title: Interactive Grid Tiling Explorer
description: An interactive tool (Singularity Design System) where students explore tiling rectangular grids with 2×1 domino tiles. Learn mode: click grid cells to place/remove dominoes and discover the parity rule through hands-on experimentation. Practice mode: 8 MCQ questions (no diagrams) testing parity rule, tileability, tile counting, and checkerboard argument. Fully responsive for mobile, tablet, and desktop.
teaching_notes: The progression from even-even to even-odd to odd-odd grids helps students discover the parity rule inductively. Step 3 is the key moment where students experience impossibility firsthand. Step 5 introduces the deeper idea that even parity is necessary but not sufficient — this connects to the checkerboard colouring argument. Practice mode uses MCQ questions only (no diagrams) to test conceptual understanding.
instructions_for_student: Explore which rectangular grids can be tiled with 2×1 dominoes. Try tiling 4×6, 4×7, 5×7, and 3×5 grids. Discover the parity rule through experimentation. Then test your understanding with multiple-choice questions in Practice mode.

step2.label: 14 tiles needed for 4×7. Try a column-by-column strategy.

step3.label: Try placing tiles — you will always have 1 square left over!

step1.label: 4×6 grid: 24 squares (even). Can you tile this?

step2.label: 4×7 grid: 28 squares (even). One dimension is even — still tileable!

step3.label: 5×7 grid: 35 squares (ODD). Cannot be exactly covered!

step4.label: 3×5 grid: 15 squares (ODD). Both dimensions odd — not tileable.

step5.label: 5×7 grid with 1 square removed: 34 squares (even). But is even count enough?

step1.label: 24 / 2 = 12 tiles. Even count means tiling is possible.

step2.label: 28 / 2 = 14 tiles. At least one even dimension guarantees tileability.

step3.label: 35 / 2 = 17.5 — not a whole number! Tiling is impossible.

step4.label: 15 / 2 = 7.5. Both dimensions odd → product always odd.

step5.label: 34 / 2 = 17. Even count is necessary but NOT sufficient — shape matters.
Click any square to remove it. Does removing one square always make it tileable?

step2.label: Try different grids to find a pattern

step3.label: The parity rule explains why some grids are impossible
step3.ruleText: Both-odd grids cannot be tiled because odd × odd = odd, and an odd number of squares cannot be paired.

step4.label: Complete parity rule
step4.ruleText: Parity Rule: An m × n grid is tileable with 2×1 tiles when at least one of m, n is even. If both are odd, tiling is impossible.

step5.label: Necessary vs sufficient conditions
step5.ruleText: Even total is necessary but not sufficient. The shape of the region also determines tileability.

tool_objectives.instructions_for_student: Tile this 4×6 grid with 2×1 dominoes. Each tile covers exactly 2 squares. You need 12 tiles for 24 squares. Click cells on the grid to place tiles.
Now try a 4×7 grid (28 squares). One dimension is even. Can you still tile it? Try a column-by-column approach.
Try to tile a 5×7 grid (35 squares). You will always have 1 square left! Because 35 is odd and each tile covers 2 squares — you cannot pair them all up.
Another odd-by-odd grid: 3×5 = 15 squares (odd). The parity rule says: if both dimensions are odd, tiling is impossible.
Remove one square from the 5×7 grid to get 34 squares (even). Try to tile. Discover that even count is necessary but not always sufficient — the shape matters!
